utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters; good morning to the staff of the Registry, the Prosecution and the Defence counsel. I think that our activity has turned into a sort of dance. We're dancing and juggling between Courtroom I and Courtroom III, and we don't actually know when that dance is going to finish. So I have asked the registrar to look into the matter and inform us. Mr. Fila, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Your Honour, I have three witnesses lined up for today, and I shall try and be as brief as possible in asking my questions, so I hope you'll be satisfied with me. I don't know about the others, but I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As always, Mr. Fila. And who are your witnesses, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is a protected witness. He will be assigned -- he has been assigned a pseudonym and it is DC1.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to hand you a brief summary about the witnesses. It is both in Serbian and in English, which will help you to follow, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness DC1. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DC1, you are a protected witness so we're going to refer to you by those letters and numbers. The usher is going to show you a piece of paper which should have your name on it. Please take a look at the piece of paper and tell us with a yes or with a no whether it is, in fact, your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You will now be answering questions put to you by Mr. Fila. You know Mr. Fila. So without further ado, I'll give the floor to Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may we move into closed session for the particulars of this witness first of all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DC1, in the course of your life, did you ever meet a person called Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come to meet him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, I first met him in 1974, 1975. He worked as a policeman in Ljubija for a number of years. We would see each other around. We were not friends. We didn't actually socialise. He was older than me. But we would see each other around. During that time, I can say that he was a good man. I never heard from either my colleagues or my neighbours that he ever did anybody any harm, and well, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the ethnic composition of Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: There are the inhabitants of all three nations: the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the behaviour of the accused Radic, did you ever notice anything in the way of differentiation? Did he make a difference between the different ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. On the contrary, we would attend certain meetings, ceremonies, and you could never notice anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever have a nickname of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes, Krkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Because he liked to eat and Krkan -- or krkati, the verb krkati, means to eat, so his nickname was Krkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let us leave Krkan and his eating habits and move on to another area. Did you at one time find yourself in the Investigation Centre of Omarska as a detainee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the same place we mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive and how long did you stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, I arrived sometime around the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There seems to be an error in the transcript. Let me ask you the question again. The place where you were detained, is that the same place you worked in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I was there for about a month. I don't remember the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay there, did you drink the water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it from the same water installations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes, from the same taps. I would drink the water many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any change in the water before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I couldn't notice any change, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript says you arrived in Omarska in June. What month exactly did you arrive? On the 10th of which month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: July, July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just -- if the Court will recognise me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I clearly heard the answer as June and I would like to just indicate a concern of going back over and possibly coaching the witness, because in fact the answer was June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes Ms. Susan Somers. You heard June in B/C/S or in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we want to know what the witness actually said. Did the witness say June and the interpreter say July? So that is always a problem that we have: Who said what? Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Ms. Somers. Both of you, Ms. Somers and Your Honour, has the summary and it says the 10th of July in the summary. So if there was a slip of the tongue, let us not make a problem of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are going to make a problem over that, then we are going to have to look at the original transcript to know what the witness actually said, whether he said one thing or another. And we are not going to go about matters that way. And it is true that Mr. Fila said that it says the 10th of July, 1992, in the summary that we have received. So let us take it that the problem has been resolved and let us proceed. Please continue, Mr. Fila, but thank you anyway, Ms. Somers, for showing due concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to avoid mistakes of this kind, could you tell us in your own words, when you arrived in Omarska, did you meet Mladjo Radic, nicknamed Krkan, and what do you know about him? Tell us in your own words, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: When I came to Omarska, we came by bus. We got out of the bus. We waited there. I had a water can. Then I went up to the tap. I wanted to fill the canister with water. The tap is right in front of the building, 5 to 6 metres away. At that moment, Mladjo noticed, from the floor above in the building. He noticed this, came downstairs, said hello to me and asked me what I was doing there. I said that I was at my work post, working as a security detail for the Ljubija mine, and he told me that he could do nothing, he could wield no influence, he could do nothing to release me. All he said was that he would help me as much as he was able to. Later on, he was as good as his word, because he would come later on from time to time to see our people from Ljubija, and he knew most of them. On several occasions, he brought with him a bag of bread and some medicine if anybody needed anything of that kind. He would bring cigarettes, as much as he was able to set aside from his own quantity. Whenever he passed by, he would be wearing the standard type of blue police uniform, without any long barrels. So he would only have a pistol, actually. He wouldn't stay long. He would ask, "How are you guys? Are you finding it difficult?" He would encourage us and leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody afraid of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. We had no reason to be afraid of him because we all knew him and there weren't any problems. You couldn't -- he wasn't aggressive towards anybody, let alone the people that he worked with in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you from Ljubija were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: About a hundred of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he happen to bring you any food, medicines, or cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, I've already said. On occasion, he would bring us bread. He brought us bread a couple of times, and if anybody needed anything for their stomach, if they had a stomach ailment or headache or anything of that kind, he would bring medicines, as far as he was able to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember any other names, the people that he helped like he helped you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: There was Harem Mujadzic and Dimac and -- there were others, but I can't remember their names. There were quite a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mladen Petrovic, nickname Zonja; Ante Cengic. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes. His nickname was Vebe [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then Ivica Majstorovic, Hasan Djenic, and Ivica. Do those names mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I couldn't remember all the names, but they were all people who were with me. There were all people from Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid of Krkan when he was in his shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I don't know when Krkan was doing his shift and when he wasn't because he wasn't always there. He would come occasionally, from time to time. So I don't know who was in what shift and why they were in which shifts and when the shifts actually were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were to assess his conduct, behaviour towards you and the people from Ljubija, as far as you were able to notice, would you give him a positive or a negative assessment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: At all events, a positive assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to move and strike the response. That is asking for an opinion that this man is not capable of giving, and I would ask that the leading please stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila. Would you reformulate your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'm not leading the witness. I asked him one question and that was to tell me in his own words about Mladjo Radic, to avoid interruptions of this kind. As to the second point, I'm asking him about his impressions. This august Trial Chamber has always asked witnesses whether he had the impression that Mladjo was in command, whether Mladjo had any authority of any kind, and I'm asking in the same vein, the same way you ask the questions and the Prosecution asks the questions, whether he had the impression that he was helping people or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, what we can see in the transcript is the following: "Would you give him a positive or negative assessment?" Now, you should put the question in the following way: "You give." Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. I shall do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his behaviour towards you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I would say that he was a good man and that he did not change compared to the prewar years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see him after the war as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him after the war. I would see him in Ljubija, going around in Ljubija, wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He came to Ljubija freely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes, he came to Ljubija freely, and his wife is from Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he associate with people in Ljubija the same way he did before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and nobody had any criticisms to make of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fila. Ms. Susan Somers has the floor for the cross-examination. Please go ahead. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Do I understand that there are no other Defence that have requested any cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. Thank you very much. Would any of the other Defence counsel like to ask any questions? I see negative signs coming from them. No. Very well. So please go ahead, Ms. Susan Somers, with the cross-examination, and thank you for drawing my attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Witness DC1, tell us, please, what was the basis for your being taken to the Omarska centre? How was it explained to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Nothing was explained. Soldiers came and said you had to go -- you have to go for an interview. You simply have to go to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which soldiers came? Who was home with you or was it your home? I should ask you that first. Where did they come to talk to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I was at my workplace and they said I had to go there to give some kind of statement, and that they should run a check of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, which workplace was this so that it's clear to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: That was a guard's workplace, a sentry post, a guard's post in the Ljubija mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection but we should try not to reveal the identity of this witness through the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So Ms. Susan Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then Witness DC1, this is not the mine, the Ljubija mine, that you're referring to, is that correct, the place of work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Later, from Omarska, I went -- I transferred to Ljubija to work. That is also part of the mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When had you last been on the premises of the Omarska camp before being brought back there as a detainee? When was the last time you were physically working on the premises of what became the Omarska camp, the mine, before being brought as a detainee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: That was in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So four years had elapsed between the time you were last there and the time you were detained; is that correct? Is my arithmetic correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was 1988 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you just said to us that the first act you engaged in upon getting off the bus was to go to try to fill a water can; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is it correct that the last time you drank water from the Omarska camp premises was in 1988? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you have any idea whether or not any type of regulation was done to keep water according to whatever standards the law required, yes or no? Do you know from personal knowledge? You are under oath.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my objection is that he is not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. competent to the question he was asked. He answered that he drank the water last time in 1988 and that he didn't see the difference, but he can not speak about regulations, legal regulations, and the question now is about regulations, that he can know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the question which was asked was whether he knew of any regulation, so the witness can answer, no problem. Please continue, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You began to answer and I believe your answer was no, but do you want me to repeat the question? My question was: Do you have any idea whether any type of regulation was done to keep water according to whatever standards the law required, yes or no? And I reminded you, this is from personal knowledge that I'm asking, and that you are under oath and you began to say, "I don't know." Could you please finish your sentence before your lawyer interrupted you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- how could I possibly know that? I was a simple worker and after that I didn't visit the place. That was not my competence. My job was only to work there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, DC1, I appreciate that. Would you please tell us how much time elapsed between the visit by, I believe you said was it police to your place of work, and the time you had to report to either a police station or the investigation centre? Well, first let's find out were you immediately arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No, not immediately. They told me that I should report again or that somebody would come to collect me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say "they," do you remember -- had you ever seen the individuals? Did you say they were police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: They were not policemen, they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know of which army they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: They were members of the then Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would that be of the Republika Srpska or are you talking of a different army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: The army of the Republika Srpska was then in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the army of the Republika Srpska? You are a Croat, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever serve in Croatia against your own people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. I never served in any other army but the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And please tell us, when you served in the Serb army, what years and where, if any action you saw it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: In the Serb army, I joined on the 5th January, 1993. I have not seen any particular action.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you take an oath of loyalty to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. There was no requirement to pledge an oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have to sign something called a solemn declaration when you went into the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you leave the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: It was the 16th, the 16th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where were you during that whole two-year period, a little over two years? Were you active duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I was a member of units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which Serb -- which were where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: They were deployed in Gradacac and in Tomasica near Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And who was the enemy of the Serb army, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in politics and I didn't know what the particular enemy was. All I knew was from the media and the television. I knew it was the Muslims. And the Croats. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your own people and Muslims were the enemy. Did you have experiences in which you found, personally, Muslims and Croats, of which you are one, to be your enemy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. It was just the combination of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which circumstances? Please explain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Could you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which circumstances combined to make you spend two years of your life in uniform fighting an enemy, one part of which was your own people, without knowing why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, that was because I didn't want to be apart from my friends with whom I had grown up, and I thought that my father and my entire family would be safer if I joined the Serb army, which was the army in place then, and third, either psychologically or physically, I would not have been able to do my work obligation, because the people who had remained there, Muslims and Croats, had left. All people who were able, physically able to work, had to do their work obligation. Physically and mentally, I wasn't able to do so, so I decided to join.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your spouse, is she -- your spouse at the time, what her nationality was, please, what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Croatian. She was a Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you have children who were of military age?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. No. One of my sons is five years old and the other is three years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Going back to your arrival at Omarska camp as a detainee, some military officers came to your place of work and what day was that, please, exactly, month and day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: That was on the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Around noon, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did anybody else -- was anyone else asked for or only yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, they came to my workplace, and they said I was to go and give a statement, some checks were being run.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You alone? No one else they came after, only you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. There was nobody else at that particular workplace.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did they ask for you by name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I don't remember whether any of them knew my name at first, but they probably had information that I was working there. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let us go to the time when you are in Omarska camp as a detainee. You saw Radic upon arrival. When was the first time you actually had any one-to-one, face-to-face contact with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: You mean in the Omarska mine or later?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I mean when you were detained, having been told to report to a police station, having then been taken to Omarska camp as a detainee, a prisoner, if you will. When did you first have face-to-face, one-to-one contact with Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Immediately upon arrival. Upon my arrival there. Five or ten minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you go to him to help you in any way? Did you say, "Help get me out of the camp"? Did you say, "Help get me things"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No, not then, because I didn't know then why things were as they were, and I was pretty much taken aback.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What do you mean taken aback and what do you mean "I did not know then why things were as they were"? What were they? What were "things"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I simply don't know why all that was there and why all those people had been brought there. I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you, at any time, ask Radic to help you get released? I'm only asking about released.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So Radic, on his own initiative, said, "I can't get you released," which was your testimony, but effectively said he'd make things more comfortable for you. He was the one who raised the subject of release; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No, not release, but simply if I needed anything, he would help to the extent of his ability, and he did so later in the form of food, cigarettes, medicines, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You provided a statement that Mr. Fila has given us, in which you said, "He told me he was sorry that I was there, adding that he did not have the authority or the influence to get me released but that he would do his best to help me while I was there." Did you ask him to make that representation to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. That's not what I had asked of him, because we never discussed release or anything of that kind. He simply saw me, and he was sorry because we were acquaintances, and he said he would help to make me feel a little better, a little more comfortable there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then what you wrote and signed about release, the fact that he said he did not have the authority or influence to get you released, did you make that up? Was it true? Why did you put that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: That's how it was said. He said, "I have no authority to release you, but I will do what I can to make you feel better, more comfortable." And he didn't know at the time how long it would last and how long I would remain there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated that you saw him bring in and distribute bread, cigarettes -- I'm sorry, that he brought in bread and cigarettes. Did he come in accompanied by anyone when he did that or did he come in by himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: He came alone and brought us bread, because we people from Ljubija stuck together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did he assist everyone from Ljubija, as far as you could see, who was with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, since we were all together, we divided it among us, what we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Please mind the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I am aware of it, Your Honour, and I ask you just for a few more minutes to wind up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when you got out of Omarska? When were you released and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, approximately -- I had no calendars. I wasn't interested in time. The only thing that mattered was to go -- get out and to go home. About a month after that, or part of us who had been detained went to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And then tell us, please, were you ever beaten or physically abused while you were at Omarska, personally? Were you personally ever beaten or physically abused at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: As far as questioning with the inspectors, I didn't have any problems. There was no need. There was no beating. Only one day when we were standing in line for lunch, I asked the guard, soldier, if I could go to the toilet. This was around noon. He gave me permission to do so and I went to the bathroom. The bathrooms were in the hangar. At one point, two soldiers ran in. I didn't see them before there. They started to beat me without saying anything, without saying why they were doing it, for what reason. They simply beat me and then left. I returned to the lunch line then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you complain to anyone? Did you tell Radic about this beating? Radic or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I didn't see him for several days, and then after that, I forgot about that, so I didn't really say anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you terribly hurt by the beating? Did it leave any physical injury on you, any scarring, any broken bones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: There were no fractures. There were some bruises but it wasn't really so bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In your time at Omarska, did you ever observe anyone being beaten? Did you ever hear? This will be -- I will go slowly for you. I apologise. There are a couple of parts to my question. Did you, one, ever observe anyone being beaten; two, ever hear any screams of pain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Never? You never saw anyone being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: At the hangar where we were, nobody was really beaten there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did people come back into the hangar in a beaten condition? Did you ever see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, yes. I would notice that they had an occasional bruise, the same bruises that I had, but I didn't notice anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And after, you noticed other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let us agree on one point. Either you will take care of the time without my intervening, or I will intervene and that will be the end of it. Otherwise, we always have this same problem. You will say, "I need several minutes," and then it goes on to five, six minutes. You have already had more than six minutes since the last time I interrupted you. So what do you prefer? Would you like to take care of the time yourself, or do you wish me to interrupt and then say that your time is over? Or will you take care of the time yourself?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I do appreciate it. I recall that I did tell you I was going to wind up. I just want to let the Court know that the witness is a very slow responder and I'm afraid that some of my time has been -- this is not something that I could control. And I appreciate the patience of the Court. Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think we should establish some rules of procedure in that respect. Now, Mr. Fila, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, just one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you please respond quickly so Ms. Somers doesn't get upset because of the speed. The water that you drank in 1987, the second time you had it in 1992 from the same source, did you notice any difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No, no, I couldn't notice any difference. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Witness DC1. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, I just have two or three questions concerning what you said. First in the camp, you happened -- I think you have spent something like one month. How did you go out of the camp? Did they -- were you interrogated? What was exactly the procedure? Do you know why they brought you in and why they sent you out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I don't know why I was brought in, just as I don't know why they brought in the others. Secondly, they asked me whether I was a member of any political party, whether I knew about any movement among the Muslims and the Croats against the Serbs, who am I, what do I do, who do I have at home, did anybody belong to a different army, did I serve in the former JNA, and so on. There was nothing else in particular. We went to Omarska, no -- sorry, to Trnopolje. It was maybe a month, a month had passed since the day that I was in Omarska, since the time that I was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And before you went out, who gave you the permission to go out? Did anybody interrogate you and tell you now you are going out? Was Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No, no, nobody interrogated me. A soldier came with a list, read out some names, the names of those who were supposed to go to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mr. Radic, who was so helpful toward you, that he could not help you get out. Did he tell you in whose hands this was, who was the person who can get you out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: When we met for the first time, we didn't speak longer than a minute and a half or two minutes, two or three minutes, so we didn't really talk about that or anything like that. During the entire time that I was in Omarska, we also never talked. We didn't talk at all, not when we were alone and not when he would just come by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I heard you saying that - and I quoted you. He told you, "If you needed anything I would help you but I have no authority to release you." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. We didn't talk about release at that time, specifically. He said that he wasn't competent to release people from the camp but in any case he would help as much as he could for it to be better and more comfortable for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. Concerning his help, you said that his help was more or less, if I understood you right, directed towards you because he was sorry to see you there and you were previous acquaintances and he brought you the cigarettes and food, and then he said we divided everything among us. So does this mean that really you were the one whom he chose to help and then you expanded this to the others? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No, no. He would bring this help because he knew everybody from Ljubija. He brought that because we were all there together and we stuck together. We went to school together and that's where we found each other there. We happened to be there together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So the help was concentrated in the people from Ljubija whom he knew before? This was his, let's say, little group --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- whom he preferred? Is that right? Did you notice his attitude with the others, who were not from Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. He passed by in the same way. He didn't stay and talk at all, didn't have any contacts with anybody. He simply would ask, "How are you doing, guys? You can stick it out for a little bit longer." And so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When he asked you, "How you are doing?" did anybody complain to him and he could promise to interfere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. He couldn't do anything. He didn't say he could nor did anybody ask for any kind of additional help from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, was it clear that he privileged this group from Ljubija? Did the other guards also respect that you were his favourites? Because you were never beaten, and you say others were beaten. So did the other guards take notice of the fact that you were more or less a friend of Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I said that during the interrogation, when I was with the inspector, nobody beat me, but the two soldiers beat me in the toilet. Perhaps this is what happened to the others as well, something similar. I don't know exactly what happened, but sometimes I would see the odd bruise, the same kind of bruise that I had. But I didn't mean to say that I was a favourite. If I had said something, I meant the whole group. If he had asked, "How are you boys?" he probably meant the whole group. There were also guys there from other towns. So I absolutely did not feel that somebody had said anything bad Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about him. And he didn't address anybody else other than us. He would come by maybe once every couple of days, every five or six to ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that sometimes you noticed that people would come back to the hangar with bruises. Did somebody come to call them out and then they came back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. It's probable that they were beaten in the bathroom, in the same way that I was, by some soldiers. I never heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were in the Serb army from the 5th of January to the 16th -- of January, 1993 to the 16th of March, 1995. You meant by that always the Republika Srpska, because sometimes it was just said "Serb." It was the Republika Srpska all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: The entire time in the army of Republika Srpska, and I did state that I was never in any other army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, were there any other Croats with you from your environment in the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: There were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: A lot of them. Were you at any moment called upon to serve in the front, in the Croatian front?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you only fought Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I don't know who I fought against. I know that I was in the army of Republika Srpska. I didn't kill anyone, and I didn't see anybody. I didn't see who I was shooting at. I didn't know who I was supposed to shoot at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you knew they were not Croats at least. You knew they were not Croats. Would you shoot at your own people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean "your own people." I was born in Republika Srpska, I live in Republika Srpska now, and I was in the army of Republika Srpska. So I don't know. Perhaps there were Croats and Muslims and Serbs on the other side as well in the same way that there were Muslims and Croats in the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness DC1, during your month or approximate month in Omarska camp, did you ever see anybody who was superior in command to other guards who gave orders, anybody? Did you see anybody who gave orders to guards or orders to soldiers? In other words, did you see anybody who clearly had some kind of authority over some, at least, guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. The guards would change, mostly at the end of their shift, or if they stayed longer, they would change. I never really followed that, and I wasn't really interested. I really wanted to get out as soon as possible. I didn't really see anybody giving out orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So was it your impression that guards there or even soldiers just did as they pleased, I mean, that they didn't follow anybody's orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, there was something like that. Other soldiers would also come. Perhaps soldiers from another unit beat me up. The few guards that I noticed there, I know that it wasn't them who beat me. There was the guard who was escorting me to the kitchen. He gave me permission to go to the bathroom and then these people ran in. I don't know them, and I didn't see those people who beat me, before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: While you were there, did you ever see any guard or soldier, guard, intervene and stop another guard from doing something to a detainee? In other words, did you ever see one guard tell another guard to stop doing something or stop bothering the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I don't know. Such things didn't happen there. This is a group of people. Only perhaps when they went for interrogation and so on, and that is something that I don't know. It wasn't something that I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Radic would come by to bring the food or the medicines to the people from Ljubija, were there other guards guarding you in the hangar? I mean, were there other guards present when he came to deliver the food or the medicine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: The regular guards who were there, they were there. They were walking around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: How did those other guards who were walking around, the regular guards who were there, how did they behave when Mr. Radic came by with the food and medicine? Did they just let him or they didn't try to stop him or they were respectful or how did they behave toward Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: They behaved in an ordinary way. I didn't see any changes. I didn't see him say anything to them nor did I see them insisting that he doesn't bring these things. He brought these things a few times, three or four times. He would bring by a box of cigarettes and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You said in your statement at one point that you talked to many detainees, and you said, "I did not hear anyone speak about Mr. Radic mistreating anybody." My only question to you is: Did you ever speak to any women detainees? Did you ever talk to any women detainees while you were at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question to you is: Did you ever hear any of the other detainees just refer to "Krkan's shift"? Did you ever hear them just use that language, "Krkan's shift"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't hear that. Nobody in my group said anything like that or mentioned it. I don't know who was the commander of the shift, when did the shifts change. I don't know if they changed every four hours, eight hours, 12 hours or so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Last follow up question. You said just now, "I don't know who was the commander of the shift." Did you have an impression there was a commander of any shift, that there was somebody in charge of any shift. Never mind that it was Mr. Radic or not, that there was anybody in command of any shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: In view of the fact that people changed, somebody had to be. It doesn't matter if it was the lowest or the highest rank, but I didn't notice or see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. Witness DC1, I have a question for you myself. If I understood you correctly, you worked in the mine complex up until 1988; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the water and the quality of the water, what do you know about that? I don't want to put a leading question. I'm just asking a general question. What do you know about water and the water before or up until 1998? That is to say, 1988.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, I know that the water was from the deep wells within the mine complex. They are very deep wells, perhaps 100, 200 metres, and we drank the water. Not always. We had mineral water too. But I didn't have any troubles. Perhaps some people did. It didn't agree with some people perhaps, but that wasn't the case with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did the other people use mineral water, do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, the water did not come from the town waterwork system. It was water for the purposes of the mine, and we drank that water because, at the pit when we were working, we would drink that water. When we had no money to buy mineral water, we would drink that water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know if there was any kind of water-quality control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't in fact know whether the water was analysed in order to establish whether it was potable or not, good to drink or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that, but all I do know is that the -- that water was drunk in the administration building so probably the water was all right. It wasn't only the workers that drank that water, it was the staff as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Afterwards, in 1992, did everybody drink the water that came from those pipes or was there any other water -- from the wells, or was there any other water coming into the compound or only from the wells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: In the investigation centre there was no other water source but they were -- water was brought in by cisterns as well, cisterns would come bringing water in as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know what water the guards and the camp personnel drank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: How would I know? I didn't go out, just for lunch and so on. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know what water the people who were detained drank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, as I say, the water that I drank from the tap and the water brought in by these cisterns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You drank that water. And what about the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, that water, and water from the cisterns. They would either get water from the taps or if the cistern had arrived, then they would get that water from the cisterns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. I have another question. You said in answer to my learned colleague, Judge Wald, the following: "I don't know if they changed every four hours, eight hours or 12 hours." And when you say "they," you're referring to the guards, I take it. Now, why do you need to make this distinction, four, eight, and 12 hours? Why did you make that distinction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: I said I wasn't interested at all whether they changed at two, six, eight, 12 hours, or who the commander was or anything like that, or who was in authority to order them that. I wasn't interested in that. All I was interested in is in leaving as soon as possible. I wasn't interested in who the guard was, whether they changed every half hour or however soon. I didn't notice that. In fact, I didn't notice the difference. I wasn't interested. I was just interested in getting out as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness DC1, I understand, but if you were only interested - only interested - in getting out, and you weren't paying attention to anything else, you didn't notice anything else, did you arrive at the conclusion as to how you could get out and who could help you to get out? Did you give any thought to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: No. I wasn't thinking about getting out myself but I was wondering when it would all be over, when the whole thing would be over and the people there would be released and go home. I wasn't thinking specifically of myself, and I wouldn't like to leave and have my other colleagues stay in. That wasn't what I was thinking about. I just meant when the whole thing would be over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I then conclude that all you were waiting for was the time to be released without doing anything in the meantime? Is that it? That was your sole preoccupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Well, what could I do? What could I undertake? All I could do was stay there and wait and when they say goodbye, it would be goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Witness DC1, we have no further questions for you. We should like to thank you for coming here and we wish you a safe return and, return to your place of residence and to your work. And I shall now ask the usher to accompany you out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC1
utterances.text: Thank you too. I wish you all the best too and a long and happy and healthy life. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is an opportune moment to take a half-hour break. So we will adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila. Mr. Fila, who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness is a protected witness, and he will be Witness DC2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the usher has already gone off to find the next witness, but we shall have to wait a little while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness DC2. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try and sit comfortably. We're going to refer to you, Witness, as DC2. That is your protective measure which you requested. The usher is now going to show you a piece of paper which should have your name written down on it. Please say whether it is your name or not. Give us a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You will now be answering questions put to you by Mr. Fila, whom you already know. He is the gentleman standing up to your left. Mr. Fila, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, may we move into private session for a few brief moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness DC2, do you know somebody by the name of Mladjo Radic, nicknamed Krkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What do you know about him before the events in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I know that he was a policeman in Ljubija. I know he was a policeman in Ljubija and afterwards he moved to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What is the ethnic composition of Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Mixed. You mean national, ethnic?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Mixed.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What do you mean by "mixed"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I mean Croat, Serb, Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The conduct of Mladjo Radic as a policeman, do you know whether he showed any intolerance towards any of the ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: He is a Serb, an orthodox, is he not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During the war as a policeman, did you happen to hear that he beat anybody, mistreated them or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No. And even perhaps when he should have, he did not.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let us now move to 1992. At one point, you found yourself as a detainee of the Investigation Centre of Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When was that and how long did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: It was from July until August, the 10th or 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That means about a month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you arrived, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes, four or five days after my arrival.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: When we got there, they lined us up, took our names down, and lined us up against the wall. We had to put three fingers up against the wall, our hands up against the wall, and we were searched. They frisked us and then they sent us off to the garage. And three or four days later, they called out two volunteers to go for questioning. I volunteered and I went off. When I got to the entrance to the restaurant and up on the first floor where the investigations were taking place, the policeman beat me up.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: After the interrogation had been completed, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I did not go off that day because I'd been beaten up. He took me back and then a day or two later he came to fetch me -- another one came to fetch me and took me up on the floor above, but nobody touched me then while I was interrogated. Then they sent me off to the pista and from the pista in the evening I was sent to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you spend the rest of the time in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I should now like to focus your attention on Mladjo Radic. Would you please tell us in your own words, slowly, whether you saw him in Omarska and everything that you know about him during that time in Omarska? I won't interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I saw Mladjo Radic three or four days later in the hangar. He came into the hangar. I made a sign with my eyes to him. I went to the WC. I asked the guard for permission to go to the toilet and the man came after me. I asked him -- I'm sorry, I didn't hear the -- I have to send my parents a message that we are alive because myself and my two brothers were there. And he said that he would be able to send out that message. And I gave him the message written down on a piece of paper from a cigarette box. I told my parents that we were alive and that they could send some money for bread. Several days later, Mladjo brought me that, that is to say, he brought me a message from home that they are well, that I shouldn't worry and they sent ten marks for me and my brothers. Mladjo Radic I saw as a guard. I would always see him. Whenever I saw him, I would see him there as a guard, but he had no particular function. He was an ordinary guard like all the others. Now, why did we say we call out to him and call him Krkan? Well, we have always called him Krkan because he liked to eat and drink a lot. Ever since he was a child we called him Krkan. We knew him and whenever his shift would turn up, we would say, "Here comes Krkan's shift." If somebody knew another guard by another name, then they would call out another name but we knew him and we would say, "There's Krkan's shift." But he was an ordinary guard, in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Apart from him bringing things to you, did he bring things to other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Probably, but I didn't notice. He had to hide this from others, not to have other people notice that he was bringing us things.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Why did he have to hide this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, we were in a camp. You know what a camp is. It was Omarska, and for his own safety.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he bring any food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes, he did. On several occasions he would bring bread and tell us to share the bread amongst us.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How much would he bring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, a bag, two bags, depending on how much he had.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he bring the bread to you personally or for all of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, he would bring it to me and my brothers, and we would share it out because I couldn't -- this was a big bag, and I couldn't eat all the bread, so I would share it out with the others.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did this refer to the group of people from Ljubija or did it refer to the others as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: It referred to everyone, the people from Ljubija and the others as well.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During your stay, the month you spent in Omarska, did you happen to notice that the accused Mladjo Radic behaved towards somebody else in an ugly way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you see him perform a duty of any kind anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No, and if I did see him, I saw him as a guard. He was doing guard duty and not as an employee of any kind.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where did you see him stand guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Up above the kitchen. I saw him in front of the kitchen as well, but at these guard posts.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How would you assess the conduct of Mladjo Radic with respect to yourself and the other detainees in that month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: He was humane.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would any of the other Defence counsel like to ask this witness any questions? I see negative signs coming from the counsel. Mr. Fila, you have finished, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Somers, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to indicate to the Court that I will not employ the stream of consciousness, narrative technique that was employed, so it may take me a minute or more longer because I will ask questions. It will not be, "Tell me everything you know," as was indicated by my colleague. That is not a technique with which I think is -- we will meet with success.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Witness DC2, I would like to ask you to take a look at a diagram that has been admitted into evidence previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is a Prosecution exhibit. I think it is 77 -- I'm sorry. 3/77A. If the usher could kindly put it on the ELMO, or, in fact, you're welcome to use my copy if it will speed things up. I just want to ask for a location. Yes. This is -- sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, Ms. Susan Somers, with respect to the narrative technique, it is appropriate for Mr. Fila but not for you. Now you have received the information given by the witness, and it is up to you to cross-examine. If you were to ask the witness to tell him everything he knew, you would have repetition. So go ahead and ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd just like to stick with the normal question/answer, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In front of you is a diagram of what is purporting to be the administration building of Omarska camp. Are you familiar with that, sir? I'm sorry. Could answer into the microphone if you are familiar enough with that diagram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No. It seems to be taken from the air, sort of, an aerial diagram.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you know the administration building, which is where the kitchen was, does that help you? Are you able to, for example, look at that and pick out the area of the kitchen in front of which Mr. Radic was sitting as you saw him? If you cannot, just tell us and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I can't, no. I can't. I don't know. It doesn't say where the entrance is. I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Next question. You indicated that you volunteered for questioning. Can you tell us, please, did the guards --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did they ask for volunteers? What was the exact wording used, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: "Who wants to volunteer to go for questioning?" Those were the guard's words.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As a result of your volunteering, you told us in court today that you were beaten up, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I received from the lawyer for Mr. Radic a summary of your testimony, a copy of which you signed in Serbo-Croatian, and I notice you did not mention being beaten up. Was there a particular reason for that omission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I don't know that it was omitted, I don't remember, or perhaps the lawyer didn't ask me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Perhaps. Tell us, please, you were given money for bread, you indicated. Whom did you pay the money to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes. To the other guards, when Mladjo wasn't there, to get us some bread. And, of course, we would give this money to the other guard. He would come during the night, and he would bring the bag and say, "Here's the bread. Eat it."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So the guard knew that you were getting money somehow because you didn't have money, but he knew money was coming into the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, yes. That was clear to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did the other guard know that Radic was your source of money, that he was bringing money in for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever come to learn if more than ten Deutschemarks was sent to you? You said you received ten. Do you know how much was actually sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I do know. When I went home, my parents said they had sent that sum of money to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell us, please, you had brothers in the camp, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And I don't want to compromise the security measures that have been put in place, but how long -- were those brothers in the camp at the same time you were, for the same period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: They came before me and left the camp the same day for Manjaca, whereas I went home for Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Before you went to Omarska, you were in another camp, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: It was Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For how long were you in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: A month. About a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were in for about a month, Keraterm. You were in Keraterm for about one month. Can you indicate exactly the day when you were taken to your first detention centre, which I presume was Keraterm? Day and month exactly, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, I can't quite say, but the 2nd or the 3rd of June. Those two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was this the first time in your life you'd ever been interned or imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you having trouble remembering an event as significant as this for any particular reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you explain, please, about sending messages out? You told the Chamber that you wanted your family to know you were alive and well. Is that because the Red Cross was not there to tell your family you were alive and well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Nobody came at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, your statement indicates that you not only sent messages through Radic to your parents but you received replies and parcels. He was running a courier service for you, as I can understand it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No. It wasn't a courier service. Sometimes Mladjo would -- that is to say, once or twice, he helped me. He helped me on several occasions but that -- then he helped me. And later on, a policeman from Ljubija, Milan Curguz nicknamed Krivi would come, and he brought us blankets from home. Sometimes he would bring food, whether from my parents or from his own parents, from his own home, he didn't tell me or my brothers that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, you stated in your statement, "My brothers and I liked it best when Mladjo was on duty because we sent messages through him and always received information about how our parents were doing." How often did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: When he was able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How often did you see Radic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I would see him, depending, when he was on shift. Sometimes I wouldn't see him for several days. He might be at another guard post. But mostly he was standing there in front of the kitchen or above the kitchen at his post, when I left the hangar. I didn't leave the hangar every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say "at his post," was he always sitting there when you saw him or was he wandering around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, he sat there and sometimes he would go up to another guard, have a chat with him, but mostly he was at his own post, his work post, I like to call it, his guard post.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you saw him in the area, let's say, of the kitchen as you described, did you see him also leave the building, come and go? Leave the kitchen, come back to the kitchen? What were your observations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No. I didn't see him go into the kitchen. I saw him in front of the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When he came to see you, did he come alone or was he in the company of other persons you might describe as guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did he come days, nights? What time did he come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So he came openly, is that correct? Did he turn around and look behind him when he came to see you? Did he say, "Wait for me. I'll come at night"? What was your general impression of his access to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, it was normal that he took care and we took care too not to be seen with him. We would go to the toilet mostly, and meet there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would he follow you into the toilet area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did other guards who took you to the toilet see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No. The guards didn't go into the toilet with us, other guards, if you understand. There were no guards at the toilet. The toilet was a little further away.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So as I understand it, then, he could freely have access to you as he wished; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Like the other guards, just the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you -- what did you do, in your understanding, to merit being taken to Keraterm and Omarska? What was your crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: That I was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what did you do as a Croat that would justify putting you in detention centres; please tell us; and your brothers as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ask Radic why you were there, what as a Croat would make you a target of arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No. I asked Milan Curguz who had brought me to Keraterm. I had asked him why when he brought me. Halfway between Ljubija and Prijedor, he stopped the van and said, "Come on, this is your chance, your 50-50 chance to stay alive, because if they catch you, you will die." And everybody knows why that happened, because I was a Croat. Everybody in the world knows that. I was in the wrong place at the wrong time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how many men or women were on the pista area with you when you were placed there? At Omarska, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, I think you have not answered my question, which was how many men or women were with you on the pista, which you indicated you were placed on, at Omarska? Numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How many men or women were with you on the pista when you were placed there? How many people were on that area? Numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I can't say the number but the pista area was full. I hadn't noticed any women there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And were you lying, standing, sitting? Describe, please, your position, and for how long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: We were sitting. Most of us were sitting but when some official would come by, the best thing to do was to lie down and cover your head until the guard would say that the road was clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Why cover your head? This is my last question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Possibly because we were not supposed to see who it was who came by. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Somers. Mr. Fila, your turn for redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I want to clarify, first of all, were there any women on the pista at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I didn't notice them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It would be better to ask, then, were there any women on the pista, not how many were there. And my second question, did they drink water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you drink it from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: From the tap. If there was no other water, then a cistern would come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fila. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness DC2. Can you hear me? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want to understand very few things. You said that, I quoted your words, among you, among the other detainees, you would say, "Here comes Krkan's shift." Was that some kind of relief when this shift came? You felt happier about it or what? Did it make any difference whether it's Krkan's shift or somebody else's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
