utterances.text: Yes. We felt -- because I knew him and I knew he wouldn't touch us. He didn't touch us. And as for others whom I didn't know, I wasn't able to know what the day or the night would bring. We felt safer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When you say, "He would not touch us," who are "us"? You and your brothers? That's what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I mean all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Who are "us"? The Croats or everybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I mean all of us, Muslims and Croats, detainees, inmates, whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He did not differentiate between anybody or would he give you a special treatment, you in particular, or just everybody would benefit from the same kind treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No. He made no distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When you spoke about sending money, you said you sent the money to get bread. You had no bread in the camp? You could not have bread?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you had enough to eat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: We had enough, but I had been in Keraterm for a month. We didn't have enough bread there, and since I was hungry, then of course we wanted more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You have no idea why you came in and why you went out?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You have no idea why you went in the camp and why you went out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Completely? I mean, were you interrogated and then you were released or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. Were all Croats interned? Were all the Croats taken into the camp or some people only, some Croats only, like you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, almost everybody from my village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And everybody was -- all Croats of your village were released at the same time as you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No, not all. Some came home; others went to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were some of them treated badly or were they all privileged like you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. Were you beaten sometimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No. Only the first time when I just came to Omarska. That was the only time I was beaten up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were others beaten, Croats and Muslims, around you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: They beat people in the "white house," but over there, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it known that you were an acquaintance or a friend of Mr. Radic? Was it known? The other guards could see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I don't think they noticed. Even if they had, they didn't show it. At least among us inmates there were no rumours about that. I don't know about elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Judge Wald, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness DC2, was it your impression while you were in Omarska that there was anybody in charge of the guards, that there was anybody in charge of the camp, anybody who gave orders to any of the guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Probably there was. I saw a clerk when I went for interrogation, but I could also see that he was not the boss in that office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But if I understand you, it's your impression that there was some kind of command, somebody who ran the camp and gave orders to somebody; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: [No audible answer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. In your impression, after spending a month in Keraterm before you came to Omarska, was it different in Keraterm in terms of people being in charge of the guards or there being somebody in charge of giving orders in the camp? Were Keraterm and Omarska different or were they pretty much the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, there was a difference between the two. In Keraterm, when I arrived there, seven days after my arrival I was taken for interrogation and then they took me back to the hangar and I wasn't beaten there, but on the first day in Omarska, I got beaten up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But in terms of having some idea that some people were in charge or giving orders to guards, was Keraterm different from Omarska in that respect, that the guards were not as much on their own or was it the same in the two camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, as far as I could understand, somebody was in command, but who that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In both camps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. You mention that sometimes on the pista people would lie down when a guard came by with what you say was an official. Did that happen once or more than once when you were on the pista, that a, quote, "official" would come by and people would put their heads down? Once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: More than once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Several times during one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So was it your impression or did you have any way to know whether those officials were people inside the camp who were in charge or people from outside the camp who were coming to visit? Were you able to tell that? You knew it was an official. Were you able to tell whether it was an official who was at the top of the command in the camp or somebody who came from outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: It was my impression that somebody from outside had come. They would come by car and then we were to lie down and put our heads down or cover our heads and then wait until they would pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When that happened, were you able to tell whether or not the person who was escorting the official was a regular guard or was it the same person and somebody who was higher up in the camp than a regular guard that came and escorted the outside official?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I couldn't see either the escort or the official. I could just see the guard who was there with us the whole day, and he would tell us to lie down, but I couldn't see the guard who was escorting the official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question: When you were beaten, was that on the way to the interrogation or was it after you got into the room and the interrogator was there? Which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: On the way. On the way to interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Was that done by one guard? Was anyone else around when that happened besides the guard that beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No. There was only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: As I understand your testimony, apart from that, you never actually saw any other detainees being abused or beaten; is that correct? Did you ever see anybody else, actually see them as opposed to just hearing about it, being beaten or abused? You did or you didn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes. Outside the entrance where this man escorted me and after that took me back, I saw two guards beating a man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Were there other people around? Were there other guards or just the two guards who were doing the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Just those two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And that was outside, outside the building or -- you said outside the entrance. So there were other people who could see it; is that right? I mean, it was not secret. They were doing it --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And nobody --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: People from the pista who had been interrogated already, who were sitting on the pista, they could see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And nobody intervened to stop it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. Witness DC2, I also have a couple of questions. My first question is: I would like to know, did you have a birthday yesterday in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My other question is the following: You said that Mr. Radic was a simple guard, an ordinary guard like all the others. What did you mean by "simple" and "ordinary"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, when you come to your workplace - and this is what I mean by "ordinary guard" - you have a boss who tells you what to do and that's what you do. That's what I mean by saying that he was an ordinary guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What were the other guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are simple and ordinary guards. Can we also say that there are complicated and extraordinary guards, guards out of the ordinary, the opposite?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: All I could see was that they were all normal guards. All of them were at their posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another thing, you were speaking about the conduct of Mr. Radic towards the other detainees and yourself. Can tell us what was this conduct like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, in my view, that was human and humane conduct, and I couldn't think of how a man could treat detainees better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said "humane." What do you mean by humane treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I mean his approach to a man. He was ready to help a man when he needed help. That's what I mean by "humane."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this conduct something exclusive to Mr. Radic or were there other guards in the compound who did not behave in a humane way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, you see, there were many of them who treated us humanely and there were others who couldn't wait to beat us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I want to come back to a question posed to you by Judge Wald. You said that for most of the time, you were sitting on the pista, but when some kind of official came by, the best thing to do was to lie down and to cover your head. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes. The guard would tell us that: "Lie down and cover your heads."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you mean by "official"? Who was this official?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, we were always hoping for this day to come when we would be released. We were always thinking now will come this day when the camp will be disbanded and we will go home. And that day indeed came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know the name of this official?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know that official?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No, I didn't even see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question: Why would you cover your head and lie down? Why did you have to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, probably because we were not supposed to see him. We were not supposed to recognise him or accuse him for our being there, detained. I suppose that it was on his orders that we had been rounded up or he must have been higher up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that a guard told you to lie down and cover your heads. Who was that guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I don't know him. I would probably recognise him if I saw him but I don't know who he was. Those were mostly guards from the environs of Prijedor, Omarska, and another place. They would come to work by bike, which meant that they lived nearby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this guard worked in the camp or did he come together with this visiting official?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Well, the guards would come in the morning as their shift required and policemen -- sorry, officials came during the day, around lunch time. We wouldn't know who they were or what they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was aimed at finding out -- well, you don't know the name of that guard, but did this guard work inside the camp or did he come especially to escort the visiting official?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: I think he only worked in the camp because we didn't see the escort of the official. We didn't see who brought him in or who saw him out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I see that Judge Riad has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. Witness DC2, I noticed you repeated more than once, and you told -- last one you mentioned to Judge Wald, that you were only -- you were beaten only the first day you went in. Had you at that time already come in contact with Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But after that, you were never beaten, because you said that some of the guards were kind, some others could not wait to beat "us." But they never beat you, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise. I wonder if I could ask the Chamber how the transcript will reflect a response, a non-verbal response, to Judge Wald's question? It was on page 50, line 3. It concerned command structure and asking about the presence of a -- the obviousness or not obviousness of a command structure. The witness nodded in the affirmative to Her Honour Judge Wald's question and then Judge Wald said, "Okay," and then moved on. I don't know how nods in this Chamber are recorded. I didn't see anything on the transcript. And before the witness left, I just wanted to get some guidance from the Chamber as to how we can interpret that. I do not know if your computers permit you to go back. I think we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers. I understand your question and I also know that it is true. I know that he nodded "yes," but he didn't say the word, and Judge Wald just continued her question by saying, "Okay." So perhaps Judge Wald could repeat the question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm going to need assistance from "Judge" Somers or elsewhere because I don't remember the exact question and it isn't on my -- if somebody just reads me back the question, I will repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Madam Registrar will find the question and tell us what it was. So it's page 50, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Approximately line 3, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The question was: "Witness DC2, was it your impression while were you in Omarska that there was anybody in charge of the guards, that there was anybody in charge of the camp, anybody who gave orders to any of the guards?"

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think that is -- and then it would say, "Okay."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No. I just wanted the question. All right, Witness. Again, was it your impression while were you in Omarska that there was anybody in charge of the guards, that anybody was giving any orders to some of the guards, that there was somebody or anybody in charge of the way that the camp operated or the way the guards performed their duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you too, Ms. Somers. I think we have cleared matters up now. Witness DC2, we have no further questions for you. We wish you many more good and happy years in your life and thank you for coming here. We wish you bon voyage back to your place of residence. May we have a bit of silence in the courtroom, please? Mr. Krstan Simic? Excuse me, I was talking. I think we ought to have a bit of discipline here, so take care not to have your microphone switched on and try and refrain from talking when I am talking. You'll have enough time later on. So I think we ought to at least respect the witnesses we have here. Anyway, thank you once again, Witness, and a safe return back to your place of residence. The usher will now escort you out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC2
utterances.text: Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I planned to have three witnesses today, but with your permission, I would ask to call the fourth witness so I would like for my assistant to inform the unit to bring the fourth witness, because if we proceed at this rate, we will finish with the third witness and then we could start with the fourth. I have a total of nine witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I should like to suggest is to take a lunch break now at this point. I think this is an opportune moment, and you will have the opportunity of doing what you wish to do. So have lunch and do your work but let us take our 50-minute lunch break now and we will see afterwards. You could also prepare your fifth witness as well. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.20 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Fila. Who is your next witness, your fourth witness? Have you also prepared your fifth witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please come closer to the microphone. The usher will show you a piece of paper, and you will see a name on that piece of paper, your name. Please respond with yes or no whether this is your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much for coming. You will now respond to questions posed by Mr. Fila, who is standing on your left side. Mr. Fila, if you are ready, and if the usher doesn't disturb you too much, you can begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 1.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. I should like to thank you for saying that the matter had been settled, that the problem had been resolved. Thank you for that. And without further ado, I give the floor to Mr. Fila again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope we are still in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We have to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Mladjo Radic before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who was he and what did he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: He was a police officer in Ljubija since 1974.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: He was just a regular police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes, regular police officer.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: It was mixed. There were Muslims, Serbs, Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In his work, did he show any kind of enmity or antagonism towards any of those three ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: As you know, he was a Serb and an orthodox Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he use force in his work as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Krkan.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Because he ate a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, excuse me for interrupting you. I don't know, but it seems to me that we still have a minor technical problem. When we hear the voice of the witness, DC3, his voice is so loud that we don't hear the interpreters. So the question is: Is it possible now to turn down the volume of the witness's microphone? I don't know if the technicians are following our working conditions right now and if they have any possibility of correcting this problem. I think that the technicians can read on the transcript what I have said, so they are now informed about the problem. Shall we continue to see if there are any changes or any improvements? Mr. Fila, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During the war, did you find yourself at some point as a detainee in the investigation centre in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: At the beginning of the July in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting. Nothing has changed. It's quite impossible. It's a pity, but I simply cannot understand B/C/S. We cannot continue with our work because we cannot hear the voice of the interpreters. The volume of the witness is so overwhelming, overpowering, that it's not possible to listen to the interpreters. So we can't really continue in this way. I think that we have found a solution. However, I didn't change anything, but I think somebody did fix things. Mr. Fila, I really apologise. Shall we try again?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How long did you spend at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Until it was disbanded, until the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you please tell us in your own words, without my further interruption, describe whether you met Mladjo Radic at Omarska, when, however, and what happened there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: When I arrived at Omarska at the beginning of July 1992, we arrived there at about 2.00 in the afternoon. I saw Rado Mladic [sic] for the first time that day at 8.00 in the evening in front of the garage where we were held. At 8.00, when he came to see us people from Ljubija, because mostly on that day the people who were detained there were people from Ljubija, so from 8.00 in the evening he remained with us, talking with us all night, chatting. After that, since it was Saturday and then Sunday, the investigative judge wasn't working on those days but he was working on a Monday, so the ten of us went to be interrogated. I was -- after the interrogation, I was sent to the so-called "white house." I spent six days there. On the sixth day, Rade Mladic [sic] saw me at the "white house," and he transferred me from that "white house" to a room that was called Room 25. We all know what the "white house" was like. He would give us food, medicines, as much as he was able to. He was just a regular police officer there like all the other police officers, except that the people from Ljubija called him Krkan, and when he would come on duty, we would simply say, "Krkan's shift is coming," but he was a police officer just like any other police officer.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Those events in connection with four military police officers and yourself --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: One day, four military police officers came to Room 25, and since I didn't bow my head, they brought me out into the corridor and started to beat me. When they had knocked me down to the ground, one of those four military police officers took out his pistol, saying that allegedly I cursed their Chetnik mothers. At that moment, when he had taken his pistol out, Mladjo came by, and he asked who had given them permission to enter. There was an argument between those four police officers and him, and he told me, "Go back to your room." I went back to my room and they remained there and their quarrel continued.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he talk about Serbdom when he was talking about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes. He said, "Is this how you defend Serbdom? If you're in the army, you have to go to the front. Don't bring the war in here."

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In order to clarify things, those four persons were soldiers, not military police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Soldiers of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... soldiers --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Soldiers, so-called military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mladjo Radic was what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: He was a civilian police officer.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In connection with the "white house," do you know whether Mladjo Radic helped anybody else to get out of there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes. He helped a lot of people from Ljubija. For example, he helped me. Then he helped Muharem Muhadzic, Mladen Petrovic, Ante Perkovic, Drago Perkovic, Koka Rade, Junuz Sauric, Ivica Besic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Does the name Ivo Kukavica tell you something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Ivo Kukavica, yes, I think that was his name. His name was Ivo Kukavica.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did Mladjo Radic have anything to do with him? Did he help him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes, he helped him, but he couldn't take out a lot of people at once from the "white house." He would take people out when he had the opportunity, one or two people.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he bring Kukavica out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he have any injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes. He had injuries on his hands.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he receive any kind of medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes. There was a doctor in Room 25, a Muslim. I've forgotten his name right now.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who brought the doctor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Mladjo brought him.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In order to finish this, how would you assess the conduct of Mladjo Radic towards the people in Ljubija and towards you personally during your stay at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Well, to tell you truthfully, as much as it was in his power, that was how much he helped. He brought medicines to a lot of people. He brought medicines to Mladen Petrovic, food.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: These were all prisoners who were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Well, there were Serbs too, but since he knew us from Ljubija, mostly he would come to us. Maybe he helped others as well but I know about us, the people from Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How many of you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: In one room? There were about 130 of us from Ljubija, 120.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he help everybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Well, he helped those that he could help.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: My last question. Did you drink water and where did you drink it from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you about the water. There would be power cuts frequently. When there were power cuts, there was no electricity, there would be no water, and then they would bring water in cisterns.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And when there was electricity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: When there was electricity, then we would drink water from the taps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Those are all of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do other counsel for the Defence have questions for this witness? I see that they don't. Very well. Mr. Waidyaratne, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness DC3, were there any other family members of your family detained at the Omarska Investigation Centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Before you were brought to Omarska, were you taken to Prijedor barracks after you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: On May 22nd I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Answer yes or no because we have limited time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: From the Prijedor barracks were you taken to the camp Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: We were taken there from Ljubija, and we were escorted by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Keraterm? How long were you detained in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: For 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you beaten in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: After you were arrested and taken to the barracks and the camp Keraterm and then after that to Omarska camp, did anyone tell you as to why you were arrested and why you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: That is precisely the problem. When we were brought to Keraterm from the barracks there were no charges against 13 of us at all. So we complained at Keraterm. "Why are we detained when there are no charges against us?" Then one day they came to us and they told us at Keraterm that buses will come to get us, that we will be taken to Ljubija for questioning. Two buses arrived. The people from Ljubija were taken to these buses. We went to Ljubija and then we went to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So nobody told you as to why you were arrested and you were not released. You were taken to Omarska and detained. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness DC3, the incident that you spoke of that happened immediately after your arrival, the day that you arrived, Mr. Radic spent the night with you in the place that you were detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And he was chatting to you the whole night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: He was wearing a police uniform and he was armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And no other guards came into the room, the place that you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No, not that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Any other nights did the guards come into the room, the place that you were detained, and did anything happen to you or any others who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Six police officers that were there, these were refugees from Croatia, I mean, the police officers. So they fled and they joined together with the army. The army had points around the Omarska camp, and they would come into the camp and they would take people out. I can't say now that there were no beatings and abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at the place that you spoke to Mr. Krkan or Mr. Radic, the garage, as you referred to, did guards come and beat people in that room? I'm talking about the guards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: The army would come dressed in military uniforms because the people who were in the garage were there waiting for interrogation. This is where people would be taken for interrogation and then after interrogation, they would be taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I don't think you got the question. The garage -- when you were in the garage, did you see guards from the camp come into that room that you -- the garage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic came into the garage where you were detained and spoke to you and stayed the whole night there. Am I correct that was what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, you referred to Krkan's shift. Do you know any others who were in Krkan's shift, any other guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't know any other names. Like I said, since he had been a police officer for a long time in Ljubija, that is where I know him from. So I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Radic in charge of a shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: That is something that I couldn't tell you because we didn't have access to that kind of information, who was the warden or something like that. He didn't have any ranks. He didn't have any markings. Of course, he had a pistol. I didn't carry a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, about the time that you spent in the "white house," you said Mr. Radic came into the "white house" and spoke to you about after the sixth day that you were there. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: He came on the sixth day to the "white house," and when he saw me, he took me to a different room. He took me to Room 25. Well, he didn't take me. He simply said, "Get lost and go to 25."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the "white house," before he asked you, Mr. Radic asked you to go to Room 25, could you tell us as to which room you were in in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: There were three rooms there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. Which room? When you enter, on the left or on the right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: On the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was it the second room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: The second, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who were the others whom you saw in that room that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: I've already mentioned the names of the people that I knew and those people that he had taken out of the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And so Radic almost got everybody who was in the "white house" to go to different places in the camp subsequently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we agreed to ask questions whether, this is not a question like that. This is leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Waidyaratne, you need to reformulate your question because you actually made an affirmative statement but only added a question mark at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic was able -- according to what you said today, Mr. Radic was able to get many prisoners who were detained in the "white house" to go to other places. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when he came to the "white house" to get you, did you earlier contact him when you were in the "white house"? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: I told you, the first time that I saw him at Omarska, it was in front of the garage. The second time was in the "white house." The third time, it was in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: This is what -- so the second time when he saw you in the "white house," did he tell you as to how he knew that you were in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No. He was making his rounds. He was making the rounds, just like many other guards did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, before we leave the "white house," did you see any other prisoners with injuries in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Ivo Kukavica, Ivica Besic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, you said that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that you liked to get away from the "white house." Was it because it was a place where they beat people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any beatings taking place in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you recognise any persons who were beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I didn't recognise them because these were refugees from Croatia who were wearing these clothes. Civilians would barge in, the army would barge in. Unfortunately, I didn't know any of those people. I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see the guards in the camp when these things happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: I only saw them being taken out of the "white house" and then being returned later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So the guards who worked in the camp were the people who brought the people to the "white house" and took them out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No. We are not understanding one another. In the "white house," there were these six guards. They did that. If they wanted to abuse somebody or beat them, they would take them out of the "white house", they would do that, and then they would return them again to the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did these people whom you refer to as the people who beat people stay there the six days that you stayed there or was it only one or two days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: There were shifts. The first shift was from 7.00 in the morning to 7.00 in the evening. The second shift from 7.00 in the evening to 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, I think -- I'm asking about the six people whom you said that -- who beat people. Were they also worked in this shift? Did they work in the shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Which shift? Did you know in which shift they worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: There were three shifts. Three shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know in which -- what are these three shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what you mean, which shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you call these shifts by any name or did you know anybody who was in charge of the shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: As I've already said, I don't know who was in charge or how you would work that out, but since we knew Mladjo, then we would say, "Mladjo's shift" because he was the only person that we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, when Mr. Radic took you away from the "white house," were the six guards that you referred to who beat people, were they there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: There were only two of them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did they stop Mr. Radic taking you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: I don't know what happened outside because they were outside in front of the "white house," so I don't know what was happening outside. I don't know if they were quarrelling or something like that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, then you were taken to Room 25. This Room 25 was in the hangar building, am I correct, the big building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No. Room 25 was on the floor above the hangar, on the higher floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Correct. What I'm trying to say, it was in the big building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the big building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You spoke about a beating by four military police officers, and you said that Mr. Radic came and asked you to go and you were able to leave that place and go to your room. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you sustain any injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes, from those four military police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And you knew that thereafter those four police officers left that place after Mr. Radic came there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: He quarrelled with them first and then he went away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it's not fair to use a difference in terms when we're talking about this. The witness is speaking about military police officers and Mr. Waidyaratne is speaking about police officers. These are two different things and this is not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would rephrase that at the request of Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The four military police officers left after Mr. Radic came and asked you to go to the room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: I repeat once more: He had a quarrel with them and he told them, "This is not how you defend Serbdom," and he told me to go back to my room, and they were arguing in the corridor. The door was very close by to where this was happening and there was a fight in front of the door, and they continued to quarrel for a little longer and then they went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about a doctor who treated Ivo, and you said that it was a Muslim doctor. Was he a detainee at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was this Dr. Esad Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think it is him. I think so, but I'm not sure. I know that he was a Muslim by faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Waidyaratne. Are there any more questions, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, two questions. How does the witness assess the significance of the fact that Mr. Mladjo Radic took him out of the "white house"? Did he help him by doing that and why? What is his opinion about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: How did he help him?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The significance of that, the fact that you were transferred from the "white house" to Room 25.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: He saved my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When those four police officers, military police officers, beat you in front of the door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you said that Mladjo Radic was a civilian police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was a civilian police officer capable of ordering a military police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Well, a civilian police officer couldn't tell even a plain soldier anything because they really wouldn't listen to him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I would have objected before this. He was asking for an opinion, Your Honour, but Mr. Fila, he always gets away very quickly. There is no purpose now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne, you know what my answer to that would be. You accuse one another of things that you both do. So, yes, it is true that Mr. Fila did ask the witness about his opinion, his impression. So we're still on the level of facts. You can ask me what I think about a certain thing. So we're talking about facts. But in any case, there is no problem. This is something that is now in the record. Judge Riad, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness DC3. I can't say your name. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too, Your Honour. I hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You just said at the end of your testimony that Mr. Radic saved your life. Now, did you know him -- I understood - perhaps I am wrong - that you met him for the first time before the garage when you came. You had no previous acquaintance. Was that right? You were not friends before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: We were friends in Ljubija while he worked there, and we'd known each other ever since he was a policeman there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. You knew each other. Do you have any recollection that he might have saved other people's lives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Whoever he took out of the "white house," he saved them, their lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Does that mean that anybody in the "white house" was almost exposed to death?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: They were because many would come in, would storm that "white house." Even civilians came from outside and they beat the people. The military came, the military that held points round about, they beat people too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And did you not go to Room 25?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, other rooms were safe and only the "white house" was the place where people were under great danger; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Well, none of the rooms were safe, but the "white house" was the worst.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the people chosen for the "white house" were chosen according to a certain criterion or just anybody would just be thrown there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: How do you mean "anyone," "anybody"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, if it was the most dangerous place, I mean, were the people in it more -- let's say have a greater guilt or accusation in the eyes of the camp? Why would they put somebody in the "white house" and not another? Just at random, if you understand me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge, up there when you went for questioning, up on the floor above, that was where the questioning was and there was a commission there, a committee, and they would distribute the people, say where you were to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was this committee which sent you to the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And Mr. Radic was able to get you out of the "white house" in spite of the order of the committee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: The committee never went around anything, they just questioned, and he clandestinely, as far as he was able to, helped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. You said he helped other people. You mentioned Kukavica, you mentioned Vlado. All these people were from, Ljubija; was that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So he always took care of the people especially from this village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Well, because we were friends up there, when he was a policeman, he met many people from Ljubija, the inhabitants of Ljubija and Velika Ljubija. It's a small place and people were friendly there, despite the fact that the population was mixed. And he liked being friends with people. He was friends with the hunters. He went hunting with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you notice his attitude with others who were not from Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness DC3, I understood you to answer Judge Riad's question about who decided whether somebody went to the "white house" or not as saying that it was the interrogators or the questioners that decided if somebody went to the "white house." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So when you first came to the camp, you told us how you spent the first night in the hangar with your fellow villagers and Mr. Radic. How long before you got to be interrogated? About how long before you were called to be interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: I said they don't work on Saturdays and Sundays, the interrogators didn't work on the weekend, so it was Monday, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: After your interrogation, were you then moved to the "white house" or did you go back to the hangar after the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No. After I was interrogated, I was immediately transferred to the "white house" because you didn't go to the hangar any more, to the garage. The people who were detained there were just those who hadn't been interrogated yet, who hadn't gone out for questioning yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You said in your statement here that the building called the "glass house" was under protection and detainees there got better treatment and you wanted to be transferred there. And you were transferred there, is that right? At some point, were you transferred to the "glass house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: I wasn't in the "glass house." In the "glass house" people were protected. That is to say, people like doctors, engineers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, okay. So you never asked anybody to be transferred there yourself? You said you wanted to be transferred there but you never were. You never asked anybody, is that right, to be transferred to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You said it was under protection. Under whose protection, do you know? I mean, who protected the people there so they wouldn't be mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: The guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, but who decided if somebody would go into the "glass house" and make sure that nothing happened to them there? Was it the interrogators? Or who decided somebody would go to the "glass house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: The committee doing the questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You said in your statement that you told us that doctors, engineers, and priests were in the -- were held in the "glass house". You said also, "I also saw the Catholic priest, Stipo Sosic, who enjoyed full protection in the "glass house" and was treated well. However, when he left, he wrote a book in which he lied about Radic, which he as a priest cannot be proud of." How did you know about that? I mean, did you -- you said you saw the priest there and that he enjoyed full protection and was treated well but then he wrote a book in which he lied about Radic. Can you tell us some more about that? How you would know that? On what basis did you say that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: The priest, when I was with him that year, there were no cigarettes that year. It was difficult to come by cigarettes and, on one occasion, he took out a packet of Kent cigarettes and gave us the packet to divide up amongst ourselves. And in his book -- I read his book, I read his book. And there are two people who are still alive, and he in fact proclaimed them killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What did he say about Mr. Radic in his book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: He said the worst.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What is the worst?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Rape, maltreatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And you say in your statement he lied. How do you know -- on what basis do you know that he lied about what he said in the book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: I can't remember the names now, the names of those two men whom he said had been killed, were dead, and on the basis of that, I think that what he wanted to do was to earn some money with the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Again, my last question. You say in the statement he wrote a book in which he lied about Radic. Now you say that he lied -- you know he lied because he said two men were dead who were not dead. Did he say what -- how did he connect those two men with Radic? How did he lie about Radic? Did he say Radic abused those men or killed them or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, in that book, he said that Radic was the camp commander. However, he was not the commander. He was an ordinary policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DC3, I too have several questions for you. You said at one given moment that as long as he was able to, he brought food, medicines and so on, and you were referring to Radic. Do you remember having said that? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you mean to say when he said, as long as he was able to, as long as he had the power to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Because they were afraid to bring us anything, to bring us food, medicines, and other things we needed. They were forbidden. They were even forbidden to talk to us, but whenever he could, he seized the occasion and helped us. Several times, from home, that is to say, people would come to his home and bring packages for us, and I can't remember the name of an engineer whom he brought a package of food to, and a change of clothing. So I know that that happened in Room 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DC3, when you say that he was afraid, who was he afraid of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: The army, the military, whatever you like to call it, because they were around at the different points and they forbade this, and they even called people who did so traitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question for you, Witness DC3. You explained to us that there was a committee, an interrogators' committee who decided which people were to be sent to the "white house," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the other hand, you said that those people -- that there were people sent to the "glass house" and that they were also sent there following the decision made by this same committee; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the people who were in the "glass house," you said that they were under the protection of the guards. That's what you said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I want to ask you a general question and you can answer it as you see fit. What was the connection, the link, the relationship between the committee that made the decisions, that decided where to send the people, for example, to the "glass house," and the guards who protected those people? Now, the relationship between the guards and the committee, what was this relationship? What were the ties between the two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Well, that committee probably assigned those people to be protected down there because everything went via the investigators and via the committee. Everything passed through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness DC3. Now, imagine that I am the committee and I am telling -- I say that a person has to go to the next-door room, and you, for example, you are a guard and you are protecting that -- are you protecting the person whom I sent there? Now, what is the relationship between you and me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: I don't understand that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we agreeing? Do you follow my directives? Are you my subordinate or are you my superior? If I send the people somewhere and you protect those people that I have sent to that place, what is the relationship between us two? Do you understand my question? Did you observe, did you see something, for example, the committee tell the guards, "Be careful, you are protecting -- it is your job to protect that person," or did you see something else, something that could explain or lead you to understand that relationship between the committee and the guards themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Perhaps there was some bribery involved. Perhaps it was friendship. Because when we went to eat, the route we passed through, there was a "glass house," a sort of summer garden, greenhouse, and it had glass round it, and they had the right to go out into this greenhouse, this "glass house," and to sit there, have a smoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there any relationship, for example -- let's take another situation. The committee -- you have the committee, and the committee sends people to the "white house," for example. Let's take that situation. And as you know, there were people who came to take people out to abuse them. Now, was there a link, a relationship between the committee deciding who would be sent to the "white house" and those other people who went to the "white house" to mistreat and abuse those people? Did you observe anything, did you notice anything that could explain this system, this relationship, if it existed? Do you understand what I'm asking you? Now, let us suppose that I have a problem. I have a problem and I wish to understand it, to resolve that problem. Was there a relationship?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Well, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask you another thing now. Is it logical -- do you think my question is logical? That is to say, to know that there is a committee sending people to the "white house," there are other people to come and abuse those people in the "white house." Is there any link between the committee and the people going to abuse these other people? Is that a logical question, a logical assumption? Is there any link there do you think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: All I know is that that committee said who was going to be sent where. Now, as to the links, ties between the guards and that committee, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm going to ask you a very concrete question, Witness DC3. You know and you observe that the committee -- it was the committee that sent you to the "white house." You noticed that very well. Then you noticed that there were people who came to take people out of the "white house" to abuse them. Now, did you think about that? Did you ask yourself that question? Did you say to yourself, Ah, the committee authorised those people to come, or did you look at that question in a more general way and say, Who authorised those people to take me out of here when the committee sent me to the "white house"? Have you any ideas along those lines? Did you give it any thought in that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you didn't. I see. Now, let me ask you another question. How did you interpret the facts that you observed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: You mean me and my leaving the "white house"? Is that what you mean? Well, I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the fact that you were placed there by the committee and that other people came to take you out of there or to take anybody else out of there. Now, how did you interpret this, before answering the question as to the links between the two, but did you give it any thought and what did you think about it? What were your interpretations of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: All I know is that Mladic [sic] came to get me and that he took me out of there, and I wasn't interested in knowing anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Radic came on the sixth day. The first day, were you interested in knowing how you could get out of there? Did that thought strike you on the first day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: Of course it did. Of course I was interested, because that was the worst thing that could happen to you, to be put in there. I told you what happened to people who were put in there. And I prayed to God that somebody would save me from there, get me out of there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Witness. We have no further questions for you. We thank you very much. I see Mr. Fila on his feet. Mr. Fila, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it isn't a question, it is an intervention I wish to make. The witness said that from the garage, that they took him from the garage to the interrogation and from there to the "white house." Judge Wald asked him whether he went to the "white house" from the hangar. Just to clear this up so that it doesn't appear that the witness changed his testimony. Could you clear that point up, because I don't want to be accused of asking leading questions and putting words into the witness's mouth. That portion is contained in the summary, the witness statement summary. There was a slight misunderstanding on that point, from where he was taken to the "white house," from which particular building or premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us do it another way, if Judge Wald agrees, of course. I will give Mr. Fila the opportunity of asking the question directly himself and then the same right to the Prosecution to ask any additional question if they see fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you come to the "white house"? Where were you first, after which you were taken to the "white house"? From where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: I was in the garage, and from the garage, I went to be questioned. From the questioning room, I went to the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And from the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: From the "white house" I went to Room 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that above the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DC3
utterances.text: It's on the upper storey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I have one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I do apologise. There's no reason for that additional question, Mr. Simic. You did not intervene at the beginning, and this is not the time and place to intervene now. Please understand that. If we respect the rights of each party, then we will see justice done. That is a rule that I have always been guided by in my career, and it is because of that rule that I did not authorise the question for Mr. Simic. So everything has a limit. There are limits to everything. But anyway, Witness, thank you for coming to the Tribunal, for cooperating with us, and for helping us to understand the realities better. We wish you bon voyage and good return to your place of residence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too. I thank you all too. It was an honour for me to come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was also for us. The usher will now escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have my fourth witness ready, as I promised to do. I don't know how long you intend to work today but I am ready and willing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think you have done well but I don't think we can begin a new witness this afternoon because the Trial Chamber has other engagements. I do myself personally too. So we resume tomorrow morning at 9.20. Madam Registrar, for tomorrow, are we going to continue our jig and dance between the courtrooms or are we going to stick to this place? Where will we be working? Courtroom I, II, or III?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We will be working in Courtroom I for the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. We meet again tomorrow morning at 9.20 in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
